opening_actions: The crone studies a nude marble statue openly displayed beside a changing booth as an unseen person sharply pulls the privacy curtain closed.
She traces one long finger from the exposed statue toward the shut curtain and gives a restrained side-eye.
Her finger stops between them as she draws her orb from inside her moss-green sleeve.

entry_bridge.a_end: Her long finger hangs between the openly displayed nude statue and the closed privacy curtain while the orb emerges beneath her moss-green sleeve.
entry_bridge.b_start: Long fingers and the same ragged moss-green sleeve visibly cradle the orb, making her ownership and guidance unmistakable.
entry_bridge.reveal: The entry reveals that discomfort around nakedness often follows learned expectations about where nudity belongs rather than naked skin itself.
entry_bridge.world_entry: Host-free matched scenes compare similar human exposure treated as ordinary in accepted public art, private in a changing space, and differently expected at a beach.

body: Families and customs teach rules about modesty.
Those rules vary across cultures and history.
Chosen privacy differs from unexpected exposure.
Context can also make nudity feel sexual.
Expected staring or judgment can trigger shame.
Galleries may present nude statues as ordinary art.
Changing booths usually signal concealment from strangers.
script_plan.optional_closing: The skin stays ordinary; the social meaning changes.
